query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the element X controls the nature and stability of the oxide scale that develops at temperatures above 900 °C. Specifically, when X is Al or Si, their lower oxygen permeability and slower outward diffusion promote the formation of thin, coherent, protective oxide scales (Al2O3 or SiO2) with minimal internal stress, whereas when X is Mn, its faster diffusion and higher reactivity lead to the formation of thick, mixed Mn-rich oxides and spinel phases that are prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy samples to temperatures above 900 °C in a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere over an extended period to promote oxide scale development.
generation.conditions: Temperature >900 °C, controlled oxygen (or corrosive gas) partial pressure, extended exposure duration to allow steady-state scale formation, and use of alloys differing only in the X element (Al, Si, or Mn).
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructure and phase distribution of the oxide scale, specifically whether a continuous, low-stress alumina/silica layer forms (in Al or Si alloys) versus a heterogeneous, voluminous Mn-oxide or mixed spinel scale (in Mn alloys).
generation.mechanism: The protective behavior is mediated by the relative oxidation kinetics and diffusion rates of the alloying element X. In alloys with Al or Si, the slower diffusion and lower oxygen permeability enable the growth of compact, coherent oxides that adhere well to the substrate and minimize internal stress. Conversely, fast outward diffusion of Mn leads to rapid formation of thick, high-volume oxide scales that develop internal stresses due to volumetric mismatch and anisotropic thermal expansion, increasing the likelihood of cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature oxidative exposures, alloys with X = Al or Si will exhibit thinner, more adherent, and coherent oxide layers with fewer cracks or spallation events, while alloys with X = Mn will develop thicker, heterogeneous oxide layers that are prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.baseline: Alloys with X = Mn serve as the baseline comparison expected to form unstable and spall-prone Mn-rich oxide scales.
generation.boundary: Results are applicable for CrFeCoNiX alloys in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state exposed to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres; effects may vary if exposure temperatures or environmental conditions deviate significantly.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative differences in oxide thickness, adhesion quality, and internal stress levels may vary with additional compositional nuances and microstructural factors beyond the identity of X; furthermore, the interplay with other minor alloying elements is not fully isolated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples, with X = Al, Si, and Mn respectively, ensuring similar processing histories and microstructures. Expose all samples to a consistent oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at a temperature above 900 °C (for example, 950 °C) for a fixed extended duration (e.g., 24–48 hours). Analyze the oxide scales formed using cross-sectional SEM imaging, EDS elemental mapping, and XRD phase identification to assess scale thickness, coherence, and the presence of cracks or spallation.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness (via SEM cross-section analysis)
Phase composition and distribution (via XRD and EDS mapping)
Adhesion quality and presence of cracks/spallation (via high-resolution microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with X = Al or Si do not consistently exhibit significantly thinner, more coherent, and well-adherent oxide scales compared to those with X = Mn—or if the oxide scales in the Al/Si alloys show similar spallation or cracking characteristics as the Mn alloy—the hypothesis that the nature of element X governs the stability of the protective oxide scale via the proposed mechanism would be falsified.

Oxidation resistance often controls the life of high temperature alloys in structural engineering applications. Dense, continuous and adherent Al2O3 or SiO2 oxides protect alloys from oxidation at high temperatures (T > 1000 °C). These oxides are the most protective, because of their high thermodynamic stability and the low diffusivities for anions and cations. Unfortunately, Nb–silicide based alloys are not alumina formers, because in these alloys the concentration of Al must be kept low owing to the adverse effect of this element on mechanical properties (ductile to brittle transition temperature-DBTT of the Nbss, toughness, high temperature strength and creep of the alloy). Furthermore, the concentration of Si in these alloys, which can be as high as 20 at.%, cannot assure the formation of silica scale. In other words, the Nb–silicide based alloys are not alumina or silica formers. Instead, their scales consist of Ti niobates, AlNbO4, CrNbO4 and oxides of Nb and Ti [,].

Oxide scales will form on any alloy that is exposed to a reactive environment at elevated temperature(s). Stable protective scales are desirable for alloys used in structural applications at high temperatures. A scale can be damaged during service, for example, scale cracking and spallation could occur during thermal cycling owing to differences in the values of coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) between scale and substrate. Thus, healing of the scale via the reformation and growth of the protective oxides is another important requirement [].
